We had many children - too many to count!
Little Mary, little Ann, little Betty,
Little Jim, little Dicky, little Tom,

He sits on an ivory throne by moonlight's pale light,
His beard is white as snow. He wears purple garments bright;
The golden tiara rests upon his brow,
While he looks down at me, from heaven he knows.

I am but one small sparrow, I know not how
To reach him here below, nor what my name should be,
Yet he speaks softly 'Behold! The golden dove!'
So saying, she flew away, my love was saved.

Macaulay's "On History" is not just a poetic expression, but also an insightful analysis of history as it pertains to education and society. In this paper, we will explore the key ideas presented by Macaulay in his essay on history.

The Importance of Historical Knowledge:
MACAULAY emphasizes the significance of historical knowledge for individuals and societies. He argues that understanding our past helps us understand ourselves better. By studying history, people can learn from mistakes, appreciate progress, and gain wisdom about human nature (Macaulays). This awareness contributes to personal growth and societal development.

As if by magic or a touch divine,
The stars of winter shone as bright as mine!
I looked upon them all, as one might think,
And smiled and thanked God I was not blind.

Like an angel down to earth he had flown,
She seemed to say, "Don't worry, you are right."
